recordings.summary_md:
## ABR · Audi factory/zone ops — Q7/Q8/Q9 localization + Q4 push · Oct 27 ~5:20p

~1h23m. Audi zone/rep visit with ABR leadership (Richard on tape).

### Production / brand
- U.S. localization planned for **Q7 / Q8 / Q9** (Georgia path); **Q5 Mexico**, **Q3 Europe**. VW Group board sign-offs still pending.
- ~$1.2B tariffs paid last year; ~$4B localization spend (rep numbers). Tariff relief pre-2030: **not confirmed**.

### Sales / inventory
- Momentum: **22 → 26** units MoM; Q7/Q8 carrying; low new-Q7 stock, excess Q5s.
- **Q7 launch holds released** — units can start arriving before Nov 2 (software flashes still).
- New **MAP**: 0% advertised discount first 6 months of a new model year; then 5%; prior MY up to 8% once next MY lands. Rewards process/experience over price war with NOLA.
- S8 / SQ9 dealer trades tight; Dallas S8 path open for Tom call if customer still live.
- Suggest DAG creative shift **A5+Q5 → Q3+Q5** (1.9% on both); Q3 Mastermind custom offers currently misfire (offer shows, rebate excludes Q3).

### Loaners / RSI
- Target lifecycle **90 days active + 60 days to sell = 150-day RSI window**.
- Need to clear ~**25 grounded Q5 loaners** / aged fleet before clean 90-day cycle; used inventory high is the blocker.
- Magna points: email capture still the easy lever (service effectiveness already strong).

### Service
- ~3yo Q5/Q7/Q8 **diff shudder** on turn — fix exists (fluid cycle + drive pattern) but **cannot quote/upsell** until customer complains; trade-in warranty needs customer attached. Daryl follow-up.

### Marketing / Lance
- Hulu/YouTube Momentum (Q5) ~15k impressions / 99.6% completion cited.
- **GBP categories** expand (leasing, finance, manufacturer, etc.) — Lance said he would add.
- Nine-page buyer’s guide still waiting finance-manager review before deploy.
- Prefer **off-site sponsorships** (CCL food/wine etc.) over traditional launch party; Audi can bring Q7/Q9 kit Dec+.

### Status
**park** — dealers/abr FYI. No Ada build from this tape. Q7/Q9 feature work stays gated on HQ image pack (board).

~33m floor meeting **2026-10-23 ~10a**. Store sales push into last third of month (8 working days + 2 weekends). Cash & Fist weekend.

### Takeaways
- **Demo drive SOP:** salesperson drives first (Quattro / free maint / service), then customer drives — stay quiet.
- **Value talk:** Audi as executive middle vs MB/BMW — balance luxury + performance; safety/engineering (pillars, AWD, Pre Sense).
- **Q7/Q9:** inbound interest real; offsite launches (Food & Wine St. Francisville) in play; **onsite launch party not planned yet**.
- **Chloe (VCA):** pause up to 30d during active deals; text **inside Vin** so auto-pause fires; mark **lost** for dead deals; end visit + mark **sold** to stop post-sale (sales often can’t mark sold — process gap).
- **RouteOne dups:** finance push occasionally spawns new lead → Chloe re-engages sold customers; merge fast; possible ignore RouteOne source (risks legit finance leads); call RouteOne if pattern continues.
- **Programs:** loyalty pages stale (Q7 still showing $2k); Q5 $1k / Q3 $750 loyalty; Q3 customer credit $1,500; lock program 7.59% needs forms/clarification; Mastermind $ vs Q3 exclusion anomaly.

### Status
**Park** — no Ada build WO. Floor ops + VCA hygiene. Loyalty sheet update is store/Lance ops if they want it written.

recordings.summary_md:
## Vanessa (Vin VCA) — customer anger at BHBMW

Floor: multiple angry customers. Issues:
- Overnight texts (2–3am)
- Frequency every 10–15 minutes
- No memory/context (re-books after visit; duplicates)
- Unconfirmed appointments → no-shows
- Bad inventory (X5 “in stock / sellable”)
- Personal-phone SMS doesn’t trip auto-pause — message in Vin or 30-day pause

### Lance / go
- Confirm auto-pause when rep engages in Vin
- Hours + frequency caps
- Email Vin tech on context, unconfirmed appts, inventory accuracy
- Re-brief floor: VCA is opener; take over / pause


### Plaud AI note
## 1. Vanessa AI Bot Configuration and Issue Resolution
The team assessed multiple customer service issues caused by Vanessa, the new AI solution bot. Customers and sales staff reported that Vanessa sends text messages at inappropriate hours (e.g., 2:00 AM or 3:00 AM), messages too frequently (every 10 to 15 minutes), fails to retain conversation context, sets duplicate appointments or creates appointments without customer confirmation resulting in no-shows, and provides incorrect inventory information (such as stating X5 vehicles were in stock and available for sale on 2026-10-15 when they were not). Additionally, the AI continues messaging customers when salespeople text directly from personal phones instead of through the Vin application, bypassing the automatic engagement shut-off. Planned remedies include adjusting messaging windows, enforcing frequency limits, educating salespeople to message inside Vin or use the pause feature (up to 30 days), and escalating backend system flaws to technical support.

### Action Items
- [ ] Verify and maintain the auto-pause setting so the AI stops messaging when a salesperson engages through Vin. -- *Lance*
- [ ] Review and adjust system settings to enforce texting frequency limits and restrict outreach hours to prevent overnight messaging. -- *Lance*
- [ ] Email compiled notes and issues to technical support to resolve system behavior, improve context retention, and correct inventory accuracy. -- *Lance*

> **AI Suggestions**
> AI has identified the following issues that were not concluded in the meeting or lack clear action items; please pay attention:
> 1. The root cause of the AI bot booking unconfirmed appointments and providing inaccurate inventory data (such as X5 stock availability) remains unresolved and requires immediate technical investigation to prevent customer churn.
> 2. Sales staff continue texting customers directly from personal mobile devices rather than through the Vin application, preventing system recognition and duplicate contact suppression; clear operational guidelines and enforcement are lacking.
> 3. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) defining exactly when sales representatives must take over conversations from the AI or manually trigger the 30-day pause have not been formally established across dealerships.

This transcript spans dealership marketing administration, an airport drop-off with travel planning, an extended podcast-style conversation on films, memoirs, and geopolitics, followed by in-dealership coordination on X5 promotional signage and rigorous CRM lead filtering. Key outcomes include clarifying a request for monthly website costs, consolidating responsibility for X5 signage, and preparing a deduped KPI lead list for data enrichment and outreach.

## Marketing Vendor Administration and Website Spend Review
The conversation opens with Lance clarifying his role as marketing director supporting Rick by managing vendors, sales and marketing operations, and handling SEO and website content. An external request (from Chad) seeks IT vendor tracking with contract start dates, end dates, and terms via a working spreadsheet that cannot be shared directly because it is “open.” Lance distinguishes between broader marketing spend and website-specific costs. ## Airport Transit, Travel Planning, and Past Vendor Mishaps
During an airport drop-off, the group discusses New Orleans lodging logistics. <mark style="background-color: #F9EDD4">A candidate hotel on Royal Street (bordering the French Quarter) features a rooftop, a carousel bar, and a pool, but only offers double beds, which they consider unsuitable.</mark> Lance outlines cabin getaway options: Little Black Creek in Mississippi—formerly a state park, now privately owned—with lakeside cabins, fishing access, a disc golf course, and frequent sellouts requiring booking six months ahead. He also mentions Maurepas and Lake Fausse Pointe as alternative cabin/campground ideas near New Orleans.

Michael Douglas recounts a stage four cancer diagnosis about sixteen years prior, how many friends withdrew, and how screenwriter Shane Salerno offered ongoing encouragement, later prompting the memoir. The memoir began as a producer’s handbook influenced by David O. Selznick’s notes in “Memo,” and expanded to personal history, with reference to the Douglas family’s combined legacy spanning 80 years and between 120 and 130 films.

Wall Street culture is discussed, particularly traders perceiving Gordon Gekko as heroic, and the wealth disparity deepening since the 1980s. Cryptocurrency is likened to gambling and potential Ponzi mechanics, with a broader critique of inequitable resource control. They argue for reallocating resources to revitalize inner-city neighborhoods by increasing education, community centers, and opportunity.

recordings.work_order: Park. Christine/Biscuit own offer sheet for San Diego course. No Coop action unless asked.
recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_c3e82526e8a764843a4d743ab5b93e1b_i1)

This working session focuses on structuring and refining a multi-tiered personal training offer framework for an upcoming business course, navigating worksheet friction, branding decisions, and strategic delegation to AI tools. The participants evaluate delivery models ranging from high-ticket in-home concierge packages to scalable hybrid coaching, while also weighing service scaling against physical gym management opportunities.

---

## Offer Ideation and Training Delivery Models

The discussion opens with an evaluation of existing marketable skills and documented client success milestones to establish a clear coaching value proposition. Identified informal and formal competencies include cooking guidance, mothering advice, and targeted strength training designed to correct physical imbalances. Client wins—specifically referenced through transformations such as Alondra, Michael McLean, and Michael Gooden gaining strength and confidence—serve as foundational social proof. A key differentiation strategy involves coaching runners on strength and conditioning specifically to enhance their running mechanics and overall athletic performance.

To productize the business, the participants explore three primary coaching delivery models:
* **Productized Programming Cycles**: Converting training routines into distinct, sellable cycle packages (e.g., priced between $500 and $1,500) rather than open-ended time-for-money services.
* **Hybrid Coaching**: Offering independent remote or local training where clients execute workouts on their own and sync for coaching support via weekly or bi-weekly phone and Zoom check-ins.
* **High-Ticket Concierge Service ("CCM" - Concierge Christine Marie)**: A premium white-glove offering targeting high-end clientele who have their own private home gyms or facilities, incorporating in-person visits, tailored programming, and hands-on meal preparation guidance.

---

## Digital Assets and Brand Visual Identity

Brand visual identity and web asset preparation were assessed alongside offer development. Website design discussions evaluated color palettes comprising orange, white, yellow, and pink, leading to a concrete design directive to replace orange interface elements and buttons with pink. Color nuances were analyzed, specifically comparing "ranch" and "poppy" pink hues against potential dark or black website backgrounds. Professional photography assets provided directly by the photographer were confirmed ready to populate site templates; however, active website design was paused to prioritize completing the core business offer documentation.

---

## Offer Worksheet Breakdown and Framework Critique

The session critically examines the prescriptive curriculum of the "Week Two Offer Sheet" (a thirteen-step framework originating from KBCU). Friction arose regarding proprietary terminology within the worksheet:
* **Costly Problem / Pain Points**: The prompt asking for a "costly problem" was translated into standard sales terminology as addressing core customer pain points, such as clients feeling lost regarding workout routines and unable to achieve desired results.
* **Economic Value and Target Demographics**: Quantifying the economic value serves to calculate the financial cost of unsolved health problems. Conversely, the "Who is this not for" section explicitly screens out individuals unwilling to commit the required time and financial investment.
* **Market Claims and Psychological Drivers**: Complex worksheet prompts concerning "claims about the market," customer frustrations, fears of injury or failure, and the "magic model" (result, condition, barrier, and enemy) were critiqued as overly complicated jargon for straightforward training services.
* **Tiered Offer Architecture**: The structure requires defining a Core offer that independently fulfills the primary promise, paired with a Premium tier (such as a $1,900-per-month package or a $22,000 annual upfront agreement) that sells direct access and elevated proximity rather than fixing a deficient core service.

---

## Brick-and-Mortar Acquisition vs. Service Scaling

As an alternative to scaling independent digital and concierge training services, the participants explored physical gym ownership and facility management. Speaker 1 expressed a preference for operating an existing brick-and-mortar facility, specifically referencing Gabby Walker's gym. Discussion points included:
* **Asset Valuation**: The physical facility's equipment investment exceeded $100,000, which Lance evaluated as an accessible, standard capital threshold for an established business.
* **Management Arrangement**: Rather than funding a full buyout of the equipment, Lance proposed negotiating an operational arrangement where Speaker 1 takes over management of the gym while targeting an owner compensation or operational draw of $5,000 to $6,000 per month.

---

## AI Automation and Tool Delegation Strategy

To overcome the friction of manually filling out the extensive thirteen-step framework under tight deadlines, the participants decided to delegate worksheet completion to an AI assistant named Biscuit. With Speaker 1 falling behind on preparation for Hunter's upcoming weekend course in San Diego, the strategy shifted to loading the raw "Week Two Offer Sheet" directly into Biscuit via voice prompts. The objective is to let the AI process the unformatted brainstorming inputs, condense messaging, and populate the required curriculum fields rapidly.

---

## Action Items

### @Speaker 1
- [ ] Formalize the identified offer variations (In-person, Hybrid, and High-ticket Concierge) into the formal offer sheet document - [TBD]
- [ ] Complete the thirteen-step offer worksheet sections, prioritizing the core and premium offer tiers in pencil for iterative refinement - [TBD]
- [ ] Determine the specific target monthly income required to make physical gym acquisition or management financially viable - [TBD]
- [ ] Load the "Week Two Offer Sheet" into Biscuit and execute prompts detailing the San Diego course deadline to automate worksheet population - [TBD]

recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_a54710467d5349a66b34b433f7d63447_i1)

This transcript documents a multi-part series of interactions encompassing automotive digital marketing and vendor invoice reconciliation, the setup, calibration, and initial fabrication of household tools using a Bambu 3D printer, an in-person residential fiber internet sales consultation, a dispute regarding proprietary fitness programming assets, and a family lunch gathering coordinating daily logistics.

------------

## Automotive Dealership Marketing and Vendor Management Review

Lance and a dealership manager reviewed monthly marketing expenditures, third-party listing platforms, and shifting search optimization paradigms. The manager raised concerns regarding an invoice from J&L that totaled nearly $12,000 despite an expected baseline of $7,500. Lance clarified that the total initially reached approximately $11,000 due to combined sales fees, service charges, and Reynolds fees before approximately $3,000 was negotiated down. The manager noted spending $30,000 in total marketing last month while generating only $2,100 in return, with several invoices currently marked as "approved pending funds."

The conversation examined third-party advertising channels and manufacturer-recommended vendor lists. Lance described OEM vendor programs across brands such as GM, GMC, Nissan, and BMW as unvetted "payola" arrangements where vendors routinely advise increasing budgets solely to inflate agency retainers. Cars.com was deemed an ineffective platform, whereas Auto Trader was praised as the premier third-party source due to its strong web traffic and integration with Kelley Blue Book. Listing fees from Carfax—which previously added roughly $1,100 at another dealership—were criticized as unnecessary expenses requiring auditing. 

Looking ahead to next year's strategy, Lance advocated shifting away from excessive paid search blast campaigns toward richer Google ad formats and organic AI search positioning. By producing high-value editorial content on dealership pages—such as detailed comparisons between leasing and financing BMW models—the store can capture natural AI search queries from engines like Google Gemini without heavy paid media reliance. Additionally, Lance emphasized that requiring desk managers to handle marketing decisions is a fundamental organizational error that distracts them from selling vehicles, particularly given broad, "sketchy" industry traffic conditions.

------------

## Bambu 3D Printer Setup, Calibration, and Initial Fabrication

Lance and Max undertook the unboxing, physical configuration, calibration, and initial printing operations for a Bambu 3D printer. The physical assembly required careful handling of the deck and the full metal guide wheel to preserve factory calibration. Following power-up, the unit underwent an extensive 45-minute automated calibration sequence involving axis homing, motor vibration tests, dynamic flow calibration, and bed heating cycles that reached temperatures between 57°C and 60°C.

Material handling and system setup were managed via the Bambu mobile application. Filament rolls were scanned via QR code on the packaging to register material properties. Proper filament routing required feeding the strand from underneath the spool holder into the intake mechanism. Multi-material parameters were verified, confirming that PLA and PETG can run within the same print job provided the nozzle temperature is maintained between 230°C and 250°C. Automatic purge cycles deposited excess waste filament ("poop") during material priming and dynamic flow testing.

The users elected to execute an initial test print of a household chip clip (using 4 grams of matte black PLA), completing in roughly 16 minutes to verify print fidelity. Subsequently, they configured a multi-color dual-ring fidget toy utilizing black and blue filaments. During fabrication, Lance identified that the included metal bed-scraper blade arrived without a handle, necessitating a custom 3D-printed handle to safely pry finished items off the heated build plate.

------------

## Residential Fiber Internet Consultation and Service Agreement

A representative from REV Telecommunications (Speaker 8) visited Lance's residence to present their newly deployed full-fiber network infrastructure. The representative highlighted that REV's underground drop installation avoids traditional deep trenching by running a narrow feed beneath the turf and sidewalks directly to a dedicated pedestal, shielding the connection from aerial weather hazards. Unlike shared broadband coaxial systems with asynchronous throughput (such as the existing Cox service), REV provides dedicated symmetrical download and upload bandwidth with unlimited data.

Lance selected the 2 Gig symmetrical plan at the promotional rate of $105 per month (discounted from the standard $129.99 list price), which includes free equipment installation and a 2,500-square-foot rated router. The agreement incorporates a 31-day free trial period without a contract. Installation logistics were scheduled for Friday, August 23rd, between 1:00 PM and 3:00 PM, with the technician tasked with running the fiber drop through the garage or exterior wall to interface with existing home office setups. Lance established account security credentials, specifying a security PIN of [REDACTED] and setting a private security-question response.

------------

## Fitness Program Ownership and Workplace Conflict

A workplace dispute emerged concerning the ownership, control, and scrutiny of proprietary fitness programming slides. Speaker 5 reported that management (referred to as Gabby) scheduled a meeting citing client complaints regarding workout variations—specifically the volume of kettlebell movements and format adjustments across six-week training cycles. Speaker 5 viewed management's programmatic review as a significant overreach and red flag, maintaining that an unqualified administrator should not dictate training curricula.

In response, Speaker 5 revoked shared access permissions across cloud storage platforms (Google Drive and Dropbox), isolating the workout slides to personal storage. While Gabby questioned the sudden unavailability of the files—alleging a need to review formatting standards for an incoming trainer—Speaker 5 and Lance concluded that management intended to appropriate the intellectual property to train new staff without compensation. Lance recommended implementing automated scheduling routines via Brightspot to periodically confirm that workout assets remain private and unshared.

------------

## Family Lunch and Dealership Operational Discussions

The family gathered for lunch at Romans restaurant, ordering beef kebabs (prepared medium) and a gyro pizza on cauliflower crust topped with pepperoni (omitting sliced onions and sun-dried tomatoes). During the meal, conversation ranged from culinary critiques—such as excess vinegar dressing on the side vegetables—to personal anecdotes regarding local church figures and film trivia concerning the *Jumanji* franchise and "Brothers Kababik."

Operational discussions centered on local automotive dealership dynamics. The group discussed staffing structures at the local dealership group (comprising BMW, Mini, and Audi franchises following the prior sale of the Chevrolet store). Staff schedules were reviewed, noting that certain roles operate flexibly Tuesday through Friday. Lance and the group discussed tool room operations, explaining that automotive service departments must continually invest in manufacturer-mandated specialty tools whenever new vehicle models are introduced. Interpersonal staff dynamics were also noted, including the strained cousin relationship between Adam and Eric, past affiliations with the Mini Cooper franchise, and service logistics regarding broken Porsche Design watches requiring overseas return shipping to Switzerland for repair.

recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_e85cee05cd698aa6bcd543c79683366a_i1)

The team reviewed customer-protection documentation, a BMW stop-sale, new X5 demand, allocation strategy, and operational follow-ups. The central message was to protect deals through documentation and pre-selling while keeping inventory moving.

## Customer declines require signed proof

A customer canceled a tow to bring in a vehicle for a tire repair after being told the requested coverage was not in place. The discussion suggested she may have tried to have the dealership cover a cost after declining the product, though that was not confirmed.

The group stressed that **a signed decline is the key protection when a customer refuses coverage**. This is especially important on cash deals. The normal printed decline no longer appears after changes to the process, so staff have been marking an “X” and obtaining a signature. Customers generally sign the card even when they decline coverage.

Examples were raised of customers later regretting declining tire-and-wheel protection after repeated flats or tire damage. One customer had paid for seven tires and blamed her husband for making her decline the coverage. Another drove on a damaged tire until little remained around the rim. The group described tire-and-wheel coverage as valuable to customers who later receive covered tire replacements, even though they paid for the policy up front.

## BMW stop-sale appears tied to a retrofit

The team questioned whether the stop-sale could remain in place until the 24th. The view expressed was that this was unlikely. If it did happen, customers could be re-signed.

The leading explanation was that **BMW stopped sales because something needs to be retrofitted, not because vehicles are being held until the 24th**. BMW may have identified the issue during PDIs and wants to prevent deliveries before correcting it. The priority is not to deliver a vehicle and later acknowledge a mistake.

The issue may affect every series, though the team must review the list by vehicle. BMW uses model codes tied to specific vehicles. X5 was cited as an example. G65 was described as the code for the 2027 model.

## X5 demand, allocation, and pre-selling strategy

The dealership had a decent start to the month. Used-car performance was considered too early to judge by trend. Pay sheets had been sent to some employees, and the group viewed the result as better than the prior period even if the prior month had been particularly strong.

The forecast for the quarter was highly positive. New-body-style X5 buyers were expected to purchase products more often because they were viewed as wealthier customers. Those vehicles also qualify for accelerated depreciation. **The dealership expects it could sell out of X5s in December.**

- **Allocation:** The dealership had 46 allocated X5s that would move up, with additional December units possible. A two-week shutdown will push much of the production into January, as usual.
- **Contracting:** If a vehicle has a production or VIN number, the team believed it can be contracted for the customer’s tax purposes. Delivery would use the actual delivery date.
- **Lead handling:** Staff were told to keep taking deposits even when no allocation is available. They should not tell customers there is no allocation, because those buyers may find another dealer and the dealership could lose the sale.
- **Timing:** Once production begins rolling, vehicles were expected to arrive in roughly three or four weeks if allocation remains available. Without allocation, they will not arrive.
- **Sales discipline:** Managers urged staff to ask for gross but not become greedy. The instruction was to make the deal and sell the vehicle. “It’s only iron” if it does not sell.

The group said it outperforms New Orleans because of its turn rate, despite New Orleans having 18 units each. Pre-selling pipeline vehicles means they are sold upon arrival. That reduces days in inventory and should earn the dealership more allocation from the Southern Region pool.

The team contrasted this with a prior X7 period. The dealership initially had no allocation, while Galleria had 20 vehicles on the ground. The dealership kept customer lists, took deposits, and refused to send its customers to other BMW dealers. After escalating the allocation issue, it began receiving vehicles. The account was offered as evidence that selling out of pipeline can build inventory and allocation over time.

## Team culture and staffing changes

Management described the current workforce as largely new. Only about 25% of the staff from the earlier period may remain. Client advisors, the service manager, service team, bank staff, and used-car personnel were described as mostly new.

The current team was praised for cooperation rather than working against one another. One example involved David finding that Zia had worked a customer seven days earlier without making contact. David brought Zia in and gave Zia the deal instead of splitting it. Zia sold the customer a vehicle. The incident was presented as the behavior the dealership wants to reinforce.

Management said **the dealership will not add people to the sales floor or flood the floor during this key earning period**. The team was urged to keep momentum, stay energized, and make every possible deal. The X5 remains the dealership’s top seller, and the dealership has a good allocation of about 48 vehicles. The group also mentioned the possibility of exceeding 119 calls this month.

## Sign renewal remains unsigned

Austin asked to meet about the renewal. Management said there would be no meeting until the agreement is signed.

Lance said Austin had received the finalized document the same day it was sent. Austin said he was printing it. The document normally takes about a week, but two weeks had passed. Lance emailed Austin again during the discussion to ask for an update. **The signed renewal was still outstanding.**

## Used-car visibility board

A board will be placed on the back wall of the office for Used Car to update daily. It will show vehicles being worked for delivery and scheduled appointments. The purpose is to let management see the day’s activity at a glance. The group settled on calling it the “Coach’s Board.”

## Safeguard versus LDS coverage remains open

A question was raised about when to offer Safeguard coverage rather than LDS. The guidance heard so far was “85,000 miles,” though the speaker wanted clearer rules on mileage, vehicle age, and the differences in coverage.

Safeguard was described as costing slightly more than LDS in one example. The concern was exposure: Safeguard may leave the dealership without exposure, while LDS may carry exposure. Management said Coach and Dan need to decide which exposure they are willing to accept.

LDS was chosen for a Tacoma because it was considered a safer vehicle. The discussion suggested Safeguard may be more appropriate for higher-risk used luxury vehicles, such as older Audi, Mercedes, or Infiniti models. A 2017 Audi and a vehicle with 150,000 miles were used as examples of riskier coverage decisions. No final policy was set.

## Honda diagnosis for the nuns’ vehicle

The nuns’ vehicle was sent to Honda for diagnosis. A brake light had come on, and the dealership’s codes pointed to several possible causes.

The speaker said the warning was not caused by pads and rotors. Those items were sold as work the vehicle would eventually need, effectively prepaid maintenance. The complaint was that a prior repair facility fixed the wrong thing. **Honda will diagnose the underlying issue.**

## Call-review roster is the blocker

The call-review system still lacks a setting or roster arrangement that identifies the salesperson. Lance said the issue is waiting on him. He needs to provide a full, updated copy of the roster and manually enter the information.

## Meeting Information
> Date: 2026-10-08 11:04:07

## Meeting Notes
- **BMW advertising / market positioning** — National iX3 heavy; little X5 beyond Spider-Man placement. Excess X3 stock; new X3 builds paused until December. Modest iX3 spend only; focus in-stock X3, X5, X7, 3 Series.

- **Meta used split** — Split BMW vs non-BMW inventory ads. ~$200 of ~$450 Meta to non-BMW. Gabriel/Carly. Eval same for ABR.

- **Holiday** — Fight Lexus December to Remember (starts ~Thanksgiving). BMW Road Home. Target closer to 120 new+used (was 107). Inventory ramps mid-Nov.
- **AI** — AI Max on X3/X5; expand X7 + 3 Series. Facebook Muse unknown. ChatGPT ads optional/mixed.
- **Video** — Add to demand gen; optional +$500 YouTube. Lance uploads to BMWJ YouTube for Google links; portal for raw. J&L circles EOM Oct.
- **Visit** — Mid-Nov in-person; avoid first week month-close. Target week of Nov 9; Lance usually Wed–Thu.

recordings.name: Consult: Virtual Contact Assistant Pause Controls and Follow-up
recordings.work_order: No new virtual-desk process yet. Timed 7-day pauses while Gaige gets definitive pause-resume answer. Custom dealer instructions live all 3 stores. GMs: VA Dashboard (texts, neg sentiment, missed appts).
recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_1da4aaca9c6814194ae606d0dd5ce889_i1)

Lance, Gage, and Bo reviewed Virtual Contact Assistant performance, pause behavior, dashboard access, and follow-up options for virtual deals. The immediate conclusion was **not to create a new process yet**. The stores can use timed pauses while Gage seeks a definitive answer on how VCA resumes after a customer changes processes.

## VCA pause behavior remains under review

Gage asked whether a customer on the VCA pause list would resume AI follow-up after entering an unsold showroom-visit process. He had raised the question with developers during virtual contact assistant office hours and contacted a senior product manager. He did not yet have a definitive answer.

A test lead could show whether a paused customer re-engages after a showroom visit is opened and closed. Gage noted that this would not settle the larger question: whether the pause list stops everything or whether statuses and processes can return a customer to VCA engagement.

Lance later found that the pause control lets users choose **how long to pause an agent**. He said the sales team had treated the feature as if they lacked control, though the duration appears directly in the dropdown.

For a customer whose deal is being worked, Lance’s current approach is to pause VCA for seven days. **If the vehicle is not sold, follow-up resumes after seven days. If the deal closes, VCA stops contacting the customer.**

## Dashboard access and performance tracking

The relevant Insights report is the **Virtual Assistant Dashboard**. It covers all three stores. Managers who already have reporting access should be able to view it because it is a default system dashboard.

Gage recommended that general managers monitor:
- **Text conversations**: Review unique conversations and anything unanswered.
- **Negative sentiment**: Treat it as a screening tool, not proof of a bad interaction. The system may flag comments such as “I bought a car already” or “not interested” as negative.
- **Missed appointments**: Managers can identify appointments VCA set but customers missed, then try to re-engage those customers directly.

At Audi last month, the assistant set four appointments. It also appeared in 39 showroom visits and 13 sales totaling nearly $60,000 in gross. Gage stressed that the dashboard does not claim the assistant generated that revenue. It shows that it touched those sales in some way.

BMW’s assistant had already set six appointments this month. It set 10 last month and was projected to set 26 this month. Gage viewed that as evidence that the assistant improves as it learns and follows guardrails.

Gage said text should remain the main focus because email engagement is weak. Lance agreed that email performance has been a long-standing problem. He said AMP’s all-text approach can remove task creation, while FullPath is beginning to integrate with the CRM more effectively.

## Dealer instructions and pricing rules

Lance completed and installed custom dealer instructions for all three stores. Porsche had been the only store with saved instructions before the update.

He built the instructions by collecting every prior Podium thumbs-up and thumbs-down correction. He also copied the “instant answers” into his agent, then had it draft store-specific instruction sets. **The result is a detailed baseline that can be expanded as managers find responses they dislike.**

Gage called the Porsche instruction set unusually detailed. He said this level of setup is what dealers need if they want AI to behave as expected. He described the product as evolving and said ongoing refinements will remain necessary as AI changes.

Pricing disclosure is enabled for Audi and Porsche. Lance said Porsche and BMW cannot negotiate new-vehicle prices. The assistant may discuss used-vehicle pricing. The option to include vehicle price in the first contact message remains off because Lance considers it unnecessary.

## Virtual desk deals do not justify a new process yet

Lance asked whether the CRM already has a process for customers whose deals were desked remotely but who did not buy. He initially considered opening a showroom visit even when the customer had not entered the store.

Gage cautioned against using the showroom-visit process for virtual deals. Its follow-up language includes messages such as “thank you for stopping in” and “thank you for visiting the store.” That could send inaccurate messages after a remotely desked deal.

Gage outlined an alternative: a custom process for unclosed virtual desk deals, with VCA included. Staff would have to place customers into it manually because merely desking a deal would not trigger it automatically. This would avoid false showroom messaging, but it would require disciplined manual handling so no customer falls through the cracks.

**They agreed no new process was needed at this point.** Lance said the issue is mainly one of setting expectations with his team. A custom process can be reconsidered store by store if virtual phone and internet deals become frequent.

## Muse and personal AI agents

Bo described Muse as a free AI assistant that runs in a separate server and browser. He said it can perform tasks such as booking, buying, shipping, negotiating, and working through Facebook and Instagram. He said dealers are using it to digest inventory, identify matching service customers, and make automated offers.

Lance said he uses Grok for some tasks but considers his Hermes agent much stronger than other agents he has tried. He was interested in whether Hermes could connect to Muse through an MCP or use Meta AI as a provider. Lance said Ada was being asked to see whether Muse could be connected.

Bo said Muse searched dealership listings, Cars.com, CarGurus, and AutoTrader for used vehicles within $3,000 of JD Power retail and within 50 miles of his ZIP code. He said it captured VINs, valued vehicles, and returned matches. He also said it processed more than 2,500 complex documents in a minute or two.

Bo said he created four businesses’ Facebook advertising setups over the weekend. For a lumberyard with kitchen and bath design, he said the tool pulled material from the company website, built and launched a form-filled Facebook campaign, and generated three new-home-build leads within about an hour after he put $100 behind it.

The group speculated that Muse’s free access may be intended to build adoption and collect data. Lance noted that Grok costs $17 a month. Bo said OpenAI had moved some capabilities to a $180-a-month premium tier.

## Action Items

**@Gage**
- [ ] Continue seeking an answer on VCA pause behavior and best practices, then bring the information back to Lance.

recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_fa9c812fc31dd4e0954c8c46e621c197_i1)

The transcript interweaves two primary threads: an auto dealership’s digital marketing discussion led by Lance (covering Facebook Marketplace via V Auto, Google AI search/ads, spend levels, and new content “feature pages”) and a long sequence of watch reviews and ownership reflections (Panerai, Longines, IWC, Seiko). It also contains personal, off-topic anecdotes. Clear next steps are defined for marketing research, budget analysis, dashboard review, and content development, plus a single call task.
------------
## Digital Marketing and Budgeting for an Auto Dealership

The business conversation focuses on Audi Baton Rouge’s digital strategy. The team is exploring how to use Facebook Marketplace through V Auto for two-way engagement: posting inventory and potentially viewing/purchasing vehicles from customers within that ecosystem. Lance explains current SEM posture and budget: total advertising spend is “a little over four” (inclusive of VLAs and service campaigns). Historically, spend was between two and three and recently rose at the client’s request, coinciding with newly launched inventory ads that have only just gone live. Despite higher allocation, not all campaigns fully spend due to search volume constraints in some segments, which caps outflows irrespective of budget.

On AI-driven search ads, Lance indicates incremental budget may not be necessary; the plan is to reallocate within existing spend. He has an SEM results dashboard ready for review and intends to gather precise data on AI-related spend before final recommendations. The immediate directive is to investigate Google AI Search and AI Ads offerings specific to Audi Baton Rouge, map options to current spend levels, and identify what would be displaced or rebalanced to implement them effectively.

------------
## Personal Anecdotes and Off-Topic Conversations

Amid business and product review content, the transcript includes fragmented personal narratives unrelated to dealership strategy or watch topics. These include:
- Vehicle maintenance speculation involving transmission issues and clutch housing service.
- Accessibility challenges at a game venue involving a three-year-old child with Down syndrome and elevator access justification.
- Ongoing concerns about a child’s behavioral outbursts and a possible benign brain tumor, with references to broken devices, pending MRI approval from insurance, and fluctuating behavior at home.
- Disconnected references to individuals (e.g., Neil) and seating at a game, plus miscellaneous household incidents.

These sections serve as personal context but do not connect to business decisions or watch evaluations.

------------
## Comprehensive Review of Panerai Watch Lines

The Panerai segment distinguishes three core lines and their identities:
- Luminor: Presented as the modern essence of Panerai—iconic crown guard, bold presence. Though some references can be thick (e.g., 16 millimeters), short downturning lugs aid wearability. The brand has also offered smaller, dressier references (e.g., 38 millimeters around 2016).
- Radiomir: Rooted in history—its name originates from early radioactive lume (now replaced with Super‑LumiNova). Origins include a 1935 commission by the Italian Navy, with Rolex supplying 47‑millimeter pocket watch bases and welded wire lugs; modern Radiomirs employ removable wire lugs with screws for easier strap changes. It features an onion-shaped, oversized screw‑down crown and a fully polished case, conveying a versatile, less “toolish” aesthetic.
- Submersible: The only Panerai with a rotating bezel; framed as the most experimental line in design and engineering. The Elux variant uses four mainspring barrels to power 160 micro LEDs illuminating dial, hands, and bezel. Across many three‑hand Panerais, P.9000/P.900 automatic movements (4 Hz, 3‑day power reserve) are common; the P.5000 is hand‑wound with an 8‑day reserve.

The narrative positions Luminor as the default “first Panerai,” Radiomir as a connoisseur’s, historically faithful choice, and Submersible as a futuristic, tool‑centric option.

------------
## In-Depth Analysis of Longines and IWC Watches

Two major threads develop here:

- Longines HydroConquest:
  - Lineage: Originates from the 1954 Conquest; HydroConquest launched in 2007 as the modern diver line. Recent updates include GMT-led design language transitioning to applied indices and lacquered dials, with two sizes (39 millimeters, 42 millimeters) and 14 configurations in total.
  - Dimensions and specs: The 39‑millimeter model measures 39.5 millimeters in diameter and 11.7 millimeters thick—thinner than a Tudor Black Bay 58. Silicon hairsprings offer strong anti‑magnetic benefits. A user preference leans toward the HydroConquest over a Rolex Submariner due to high-contrast white indices and bezel markings, which visually “pop” and influence daily wear choice. A note on value: the speaker anticipates greater depreciation for Longines (20–40% from retail) versus historically stronger retention for Tudor Black Bay references, though exact figures vary with time and supply.

- IWC Ingenieur (Aqua Dial):
  - Heritage and design: A 40‑millimeter revival of the 1976 Gerald Genta Ingenieur SL, contemporaneous with the Royal Oak and Nautilus. The new model embraces an integrated sports-watch profile with an industrial character, functional bezel screws, and refined H‑link bracelet finishing.
  - Wear profile: Thickness is 10.7 millimeters, with a central lug‑to‑lug of 45.7 millimeters and extended end links bringing total span to 49.5 millimeters; sharply angled end links help it wear true to size. The smaller dial opening versus comparable divers yields a compact visual footprint.
  - Movement and debate: Uses IWC Caliber 32111 (4 Hz, 120‑hour/5‑day reserve). Architecture originates from Richemont’s ValFleurier, also seen in models priced below the Ingenieur (e.g., IWC Mark XX) and historically in Bvlgari/Montblanc. While this raises questions about price-to-movement value, the speaker argues the sum of design, finishing, heritage, and on‑wrist experience justifies the premium. A soft iron inner cage under a closed caseback provides magnetic protection while retaining 100 meters of water resistance.

------------
## Review of Seiko Watch Collections

A survey of attainable Seiko choices (excluding Grand Seiko) positions models by role and value:
- Presage Classic: Recommended as a top everyday mechanical under $1,000, featuring a 40‑millimeter steel case and bracelet, silk‑textured dial, AR‑coated sapphire, 100‑meter water resistance, and the 6R55 movement with a 72‑hour reserve (Spron 510 mainspring). The Silk Dial 38‑millimeter variants satisfy smaller, dressier preferences. Seiko often ships movements unregulated to keep costs down; many examples still run better than stated specs, and watchmakers can fine‑tune accuracy.
- SPB317 “Turtle” (Prospex): A versatile sport diver with a slim profile for the form factor—41 millimeters, 12.3 millimeters thick, 200 meters water resistance, 6R35 movement with 70‑hour reserve, MSRP $900—designed to blend dive‑ready reliability with daily-wear comfort.
- SLA079 Marine Master: A professional diver at 42.6 millimeters and 12.3 millimeters thick with a lacquered steel bezel (eschewing ceramic to avoid underwater brittleness) and the 8L35 movement (a Grand Seiko 9S55 variant) built with MEMS‑made components and a replaceable screw‑in crown tube—emphasizing longevity and serviceability.
- King Seiko SJN121: A premium dress model—145th anniversary limited edition, 800 pieces—highlighted for its finishing and commemorative appeal.

------------
## Strategic Initiative for Dealership Feature Pages

Lance proposes building comprehensive, information‑rich “feature pages” aligned to two customer journeys:
1) Shoppers looking to lease/buy new vehicles.
2) Shoppers seeking used or certified vehicles.

These pages must be visually strong and content‑dense to serve both direct visitors and AI-driven discovery tools that increasingly guide customers. The plan is to pilot this at Audi Baton Rouge to establish a repeatable content “skill,” then replicate across other brands and locations once the initial framework is validated. Immediate steps include defining a proposed list of page types, discussing and approving the list, then producing the first set for Audi Baton Rouge.

------------

  - [ ] Analyze budget impact and identify which current campaigns/spend would be displaced or reallocated to implement Google AI options - [TBD]

> **Date:** 2026-10-05

> **Participants:** [Speaker 1] [Speaker 2] [Speaker 3] [Speaker 5] [Speaker 6] [Speaker 7] [Speaker 8] [Speaker 9] [Lance]
---
## Meeting Notes
### Improving Service Sales Performance
- [Speaker 1] highlighted a recent new car sale that took two days and yielded only $1,500 profit, emphasizing the effort required per sale and drawing a parallel to the dedication needed from service writers.
- From April to July, average hours per repair order (RO) was 2.44. After implementing callbacks for lost opportunities and offering discounts, the average increased to 2.69 hours per RO over the last two months.
- New target for customer-pay work is **3.0 hours per RO**, considered achievable.
- Writers should focus on selling necessary repairs while customers are on-site; 0% financing options should be promoted to help close service sales.
- The dealership's warranty claims are lower than the average dealer, possibly due to being overly cautious — valid warranty work, particularly related to the differential, may be missed.
- Service advisors need to conduct better customer interviews to identify and document vehicle issues properly, including prompting customers about specific symptoms (e.g., vibrations, rubbing sensations on turns).
---
### F&I Performance Review
- Significant improvement last month: F&I reached **$2,600 per copy** with a 64% finance penetration rate.
- Discussion held about reintroducing a "finance fifth" on used cars to push toward a **$3,000 per copy** target.
---
### Vehicle Differential Service and Warranty Issues
- A recurring and systemic issue exists with the differential on **Q5 models**. Cars with the problem are being traded in without the issue being addressed under warranty.
  - The repair involves a differential flush (~$600); if unsuccessful, full replacement costs ~$2,500, often absorbed by the dealership.
  - A specific Q5 has been in service for **a year and a half** without resolution; a new module is expected but no contingency plan exists if that fails.
- Technicians are reportedly reluctant to perform the warranty diff flush because it is time-consuming relative to compensation.
- Manufacturer policy requires a **customer complaint** before warranty work can be initiated, creating tension with the dealership's goal of proactive customer retention.
- The issue is a known TSB, but the manufacturer classifies it as a **"feel" concern** rather than a safety issue to avoid a recall.
- Under warranty, diff and motor mount issues cannot be directly upsold; the approach is to inform customers, add complaint lines, and manage through warranty processes.
- The team agreed this puts both the dealership and customers in a poor position and that the manufacturer should bear responsibility.
- **Plan:** Discuss directly with manufacturer representatives (Sam and Mark) during their visit on **October 27th**, and separately schedule a meeting with representative **Terrence** to address the Q5 differential issue and broader service/warranty policies.
---
### Internal Costs and Inter-Departmental Trust
- Significant conflict exists between the **used car department and service department** regarding repair costs on trade-in vehicles.
  - Used car department feels "jammed up" by high service costs that erode profit margins.
  - Example: A $500 price discrepancy for TPM sensors between their service department and an external Lincoln dealer.
  - Used car manager stated they will send work elsewhere if it is more cost-effective.
- There is widespread **distrust of service technician quotes** for used cars — estimates are perceived as inflated or unnecessary (e.g., $5,000–$6,000 quotes on cars bought for $17,000–$20,000).
  - Specific concerns: charging diagnostic fees when the issue is already known, quoting major repairs based on poor-quality photos, and charging $189 to plug in a car to charge its battery.
  - Technicians are perceived as possibly pressured by management to maximize revenue per job.
- The team indicated greater trust in independent shops than their own service department.
- No clear resolution or collaboration plan between the two departments was established.
---
### Diagnostic (Diag) Charges and Integration with Repair Quotes
- Diag charges apply when work requires disassembly beyond initial inspection (e.g., door/window fault testing, dye for oil leak detection).
- If diag requires disassembly, related repairs should **not** be charged separately — diag should be rolled into the repair cost.
- Agreed principle: **diag charges should be credited against repair costs**; questionable cases will be reviewed on request.
- Clear thresholds for when diag charges are applied and how they are credited have not yet been formally documented.
---
### UCI Inspection Scope, Timing, and Transparency
- UCI uses a checklist with green/yellow/red statuses covering: brakes, tires (tread depth), leaks, lights, belts, fluids, A/C function, and traction control.
- Inspection duration varies by vehicle and mileage.
- A request was made for a fully documented, transparent checklist of all UCI items.
- Concern raised about short inspections being billed at higher hours — no benchmarks by vehicle type have been established.
- **Action:** Share the itemized UCI checklist with the team.
---
### AI Sales Assistant Issues
- The current AI configuration is not working effectively; its benefit to sales is unclear and the verbiage is considered subpar.
- Key problems:
  - AI stops communicating with a customer indefinitely once a salesperson engages.
  - AI cannot be easily re-engaged after a set period of salesperson inactivity (e.g., customer leaves without buying).
  - The AI and sales team use **two different phone numbers** for texting, risking customer confusion — no decision was made on whether to pursue a single-number solution.

recordings.name: 09-26 CRM Process Gap Causes AI to Contact Sold Customers
recordings.work_order: VCA/CRM: sold-status lag lets AI re-engage sold buyers (Louis Delia case). Fix path = request sold + desk mgr (Chad), not indefinite pause. Side: Hunter Miller email signature by Tue (Lance).
recordings.summary_md:
## Core Synopsis

A systemic process gap in the sales CRM is causing the automated follow-up AI to contact customers who have already purchased a vehicle, creating a nuisance for both the client and the sales team. The immediate trigger is the delay between a deal being finalized and the lead being marked "sold" in the system, which can take up to a week. The root cause is a workflow dependency: salespeople lack the permissions to mark leads as sold themselves and must rely on a desk manager, creating a bottleneck. This operational friction is forcing salespeople to seek inefficient workarounds, like pausing notifications, which are only temporary and fail to solve the underlying data integrity problem. While the team debates the AI's behavior, the actual issue is the broken process for updating a lead's status in a timely manner.

## Diagnostic Deep-Dive: AI Nuisance & CRM Workflow Failure

### The Phenomenon: AI System Contacting Sold Customers

The dealership's automated AI system is re-engaging with customers who have already completed a purchase. In the specific case of a customer named "Louis Delia," the system continued to treat him as an "active lead" even after a car was sold to him earlier in the week. This is causing confusion and requires manual intervention to stop the unwanted communication.

### The Mechanism: Lead Status & System Latency

The AI's behavior is a direct result of how the CRM handles lead statuses.
*   **The Trigger:** The system sees an "open" or "active" lead for a customer and automatically initiates or resumes communication.
*   **The Process Gap:** A lead is not marked "sold" immediately after a transaction. There's a significant lag, described as up to a week, between the finance department finalizing a deal and the CRM updating to reflect the "sold" status.
*   **Duplicate Leads:** The problem is compounded when a customer submits a credit application, which generates a duplicate lead. This increases the chance that one of the leads remains "open" while the other is being processed, ensuring the AI will continue engagement.

### The Root Cause: A Bottleneck in User Permissions & Workflow

The core issue is not the AI itself, but a flawed operational workflow.
*   **Ineffective Workarounds:** Sales staff are attempting to use the "pause" function to temporarily halt the AI. However, this is not a permanent solution, as the pause either expires or is overridden when the customer responds. This leads to requests for an "indefinite pause" feature, which treats the symptom rather than the disease.
*   **The True Bottleneck:** Salespeople do not have the system permissions to change a lead's status to "sold." They must request a desk manager (e.g., "Chad") to perform this action. This dependency creates the critical time lag that allows the AI to continue communicating with sold customers. The correct procedure is to "request sold," have the manager approve it, and end any open visits in the system.

## Next Move

**@Lance**
- [ ] Investigate how to make the "pause" function more indefinite for leads, as a temporary workaround - [TBD]
- [ ] Set up the email signature for the new employee, Hunter Miller - [By Tuesday]

recordings.name: 09-24 Reasoning Note: Scaling a CRM Replacement Dashboard and Addressing Unbudgeted Compute Costs
recordings.summary_md:
[](plaud://image?type=summaryCard&id=oc_su_f682c3beb42f8e6960542e1aff46508d_i1)

## Core Synopsis

The engineering lead has successfully developed a prototype dashboard that fully replicates the core data-mining functionality of the dealership's former CRM, Mastermind. This new tool integrates the entire customer portfolio from the DMS, allowing salespeople to filter by metrics like contract maturity dates, which immediately provides a list of actionable sales leads. While the initial feedback from the sales team is overwhelmingly positive, confirming the tool could replace Mastermind and save that expense, the primary strategic bottleneck is now cost-scaling. The lead developer is concerned that expanding from a single-instance pilot to individual dashboards for every salesperson will incur significant, unbudgeted compute costs, potentially several hundred dollars per month. This transforms the project from a personal development initiative into a formal product with financial implications that need to be addressed before a full rollout.

## The Pilot Program: A "Mastermind" Replacement

### 1. The Problem Gap
*   **Status Quo**: The dealership cancelled its subscription to the Mastermind CRM, leaving salespeople without a tool to mine the existing customer base for new opportunities (e.g., upcoming lease maturities).
*   **The Pain**: Salespeople expressed frustration over losing this capability and requested that management bring Mastermind back.
*   **The Critical Need**: A simple, effective way for the sales team to identify and engage high-potential customers within the dealership's portfolio without incurring the cost of a full-featured CRM.

### 2. The Solution: An Integrated Dashboard
*   **Core Functionality**: The new tool is a standalone dashboard, not a full CRM. It has ingested the entire customer portfolio from the DMS, creating a complete analog of the dealership's business history.
*   **Key Feature**: A "Portfolio Mode" allows users to apply dynamic filters, such as "maturities in the next month," to instantly generate lists of customers with upcoming service or purchasing needs. This directly replicates the "mining" function that salespeople valued in Mastermind.
*   **Data Integrity**: The dashboard includes historical sales data, such as which salesperson originally sold the car, but it intentionally excludes new vehicle notes, as that feature was deemed low-value "silliness" by the developer.

## The Strategic Crossroads: Scaling and Cost

### 1. The Scaling Request
The immediate user request is to provide each salesperson with their own personalized dashboard view, pre-filtered to their specific customer list. This would allow them to see their maturing contracts and other opportunities without having to manually select their name.

### 2. The Bottleneck: Unbudgeted Compute Costs
*   **Thesis (The Pilot)**: In its current state, the tool is a low-cost personal project developed by the lead.
*   **Antithesis (The Rollout)**: Deploying individualized dashboards for the entire sales team would dramatically increase server activity ("compute"). This would shift the project from a negligible expense to a significant operational cost, estimated at a potential $400-$600 per month.
*   **Synthesis (The Decision Point)**: The developer believes creating individual dashboards is technically "doable" since it uses the same underlying data. However, a decision must be made on whether the business is willing to fund these new operational costs to fully replace Mastermind.

## Overview
The consultation centered on website improvements for an automotive dealer group and operational alignment during onboarding to a new platform (Bayrend). The customer, Lance, manages multiple premium brands (Audi, BMW, Porsche) and oversees sales and service processes. Key topics included elevating brand visibility on the group site, replacing the static map with a dynamic “locations near you” module, clarifying Bayrend onboarding status, and safeguarding data continuity by downloading key task and opportunity information before the platform switch. Main pain points are limited brand prominence on the site, uncertainty about onboarding progress and data retention/reporting, and difficulty exporting comprehensive opportunity brief data to power Lance’s internal acquisition dashboard. Desired outcomes include enhanced UX for brand shopping and locations, clear onboarding steps, preserved access to actionable customer intelligence, and improved service-to-sales situational awareness.
## Background
- Lance represents a dealer group with Audi, BMW, and Porsche, operating multiple locations displayed on their group site.
- A consultant (Speaker 3) proposed and will implement two site enhancements: “Shop by Brand” tiles to highlight brands and a dynamic “locations near you” section that shows address/hours and optional storefront images.
- The group is transitioning to Bayrend; onboarding emails requesting items were received on 2026-09-21.
- Current dashboard shows a 42% engagement rate, 20 vehicle sales (5 delivered; 4 pre-owned), 3 sales with no prior contact, 74 indirect leads, and 200 repair orders with $133,846 gross profit. Twenty-four sales appointments were set; 16 occurred; 11 resulted in sales; reported gross profit is “a little over” $54,000 on sales.
- Lance built an internal acquisition dashboard to cross-reference service and sales leads to improve situational awareness for sales staff.
## Pain Points
Limited brand prominence and suboptimal location UX on the group site reduce customer engagement and brand-driven navigation, leading to missed opportunities for customers to quickly find inventory by brand and locate nearby stores. Brand logos (Audi, BMW, Porsche) “get a little bit lost,” and the map-based location module is less dynamic. Context: Premium brand dealership group competing for attention; improved UI can increase conversions. Stakeholders: Marketing/website team, sales leads, customers seeking brand-specific inventory and nearest store.
Uncertainty about Bayrend onboarding status and potential data loss/availability during the platform transition creates risk of workflow disruption and lost insights. Lance has “not met with them since I signed” and “doesn’t have a clue” where he is in the process until an email requesting onboarding items arrived on 2026-09-21. Impact: Potential loss of active tasks/opportunities due to “sixty-day lookback” and unclear migration, risking follow-up gaps and revenue leakage. Context: Transition windows often have data retention rules (e.g., 60-day lookback) causing historical items to drop. Stakeholders: Lance, sales team, RSM/demo sales, Bayrend onboarding team.
Inadequate export/reporting detail to support Lance’s acquisition dashboard hampers service-to-sales situational awareness. The “task detail report” only has “six rows of data” and “doesn’t tell you anything” compared to the in-app opportunity brief with customer intelligence and buying signals. Examples: Lance wants a “more complete brief” per opportunity to feed his dashboard; hyperlinks and detailed content exist in the UI but not in export. Context: Salespeople may lack situational awareness if not aggressive; Lance’s dashboard is meant to bridge that gap. Stakeholders: Lance, sales team, service advisors, customers with service appointments and leads.
## Expectations
Implement “Shop by Brand” and “Locations Near You” enhancements to improve customer navigation and brand engagement. Timeframe: “next couple days” for visible site changes. Resources required: Storefront images (optional), brand inventory links, web admin access. Success metrics: Increased clicks into brand inventory, higher engagement and conversion from the location module. Stakeholders: Website/marketing team, Speaker 3 implementing changes, sales teams benefiting from improved traffic.
Clarify Bayrend onboarding steps and ensure continuity of tasks/opportunities through the platform transition. Goal: Confirm implementation requirements (logos, assets), migration approach, and data retention rules (including 60-day lookback). Timeframe: Immediate follow-up post-call; onboarding email received on 2026-09-21. Resources required: Onboarding items package, coordination with Bayrend RSM/demo sales, reporting exports. Success metrics: No loss of active tasks/opportunities; documented export of due-date-sorted items; clear onboarding timeline. Stakeholders: Lance, Bayrend onboarding team, current platform support.
Enable a richer export or alternative data capture that preserves customer intelligence and buying signals for Lance’s acquisition dashboard. Timeframe: Near-term, before final platform switch. Resources required: Report configuration or data feed/API, filters for “active” items (82), date sorting, potential manual harvesting of opportunity details. > 1. Establish a data continuity plan: schedule a joint session with Bayrend to confirm the 60-day lookback, historical data availability, and export formats; document retention/migration guarantees.
> 2. Create an interim data archive: export all active items (82) and recent opportunities by due date, and capture key opportunity briefs via bulk capture or scripted browser export (if API unavailable).

> 5. Prioritize high-value segments: identify opportunities tied to near-term campaigns (e.g., BMW X5 model change, “Service now, pay later”) and ensure these records are manually verified and retained.

This conversation documents the demonstration of a new sales lead generation tool called "Acquire," developed by Lance. He explains its features, intended workflow for sales managers, and potential for future customization based on user feedback.

## Introduction and Core Functionality of the "Acquire" Tool

Lance introduces "Acquire," a custom-built software tool designed to streamline lead generation for sales managers. Its primary function is to aggregate and display data from three key sources: dealership service appointments, incoming web leads, and current vehicle inventory. The core concept is to provide managers with a consolidated view of customers visiting the service department, enabling them to proactively identify sales opportunities. Lance explained that the tool was built to be a simple, efficient alternative to existing systems like ViAuto, Ven, and the more expensive Mastermind, allowing a manager to quickly "hop in" and create leads. The interface features "copy buttons" for easy data transfer to the dealership's CRM (VinSolutions). A central feature is "Export to CRM," which lets a user select a service customer, assign a potential vehicle of interest using a "lot fit" prediction based on their current car, and push the information directly into the CRM as a new lead.

## Technical Demonstration and Workflow Customization

Lance conducted a live demonstration of the "Acquire" tool, showcasing its direct integration with the dealership's VIN Solutions CRM. He explained that when a lead is created through the tool, it is automatically tagged with the source "acquire service," allowing for specific tracking and process automation. During a test, they successfully exported a service customer's information, creating an active lead in the CRM almost instantly. A key discussion point arose regarding lead assignment. While the tool allows a user to select a salesperson, it was determined that the system cannot currently force-assign a lead or override the CRM's established lead-routing rules, as it is not a native Cox product and lacks that level of authorization. Instead, it adheres to the default parameters, like a standard web lead. The group also considered an alternative workflow where individual salespeople could be given access to the tool, empowering them to "filter themselves" and proactively identify opportunities from the service drive, rather than relying solely on managers to assign leads.

## Feature Requests and Future Development Roadmap

The team provided several key feature requests to enhance the "Acquire" tool's utility for the Porsche-specific environment. The most significant request was to import the dealership's entire customer file to enable deep searchability. This would allow a salesperson to, for example, search for all current owners of a specific model like the Panamera or 911 when a new model arrives. Another suggestion was to add a field on the main dashboard to display the original salesperson who sold the car to the service customer, facilitating a natural and informed follow-up. The group also discussed the need to digitize and integrate physical lead sheets provided by Porsche Financial Services (PFS). Lance affirmed his ability to implement these features rapidly and positioned the users as early adopters in a beta phase.

## Data Sourcing and Integration Challenges

PCNA and PFS operate as distinct legal entities and do not share data due to privacy laws. Lease maturity and finance leads arrive on paper, not as digital files. Agreed workaround: store scans monthly physical PFS lead sheets and emails the PDF to Lance; Ada extracts and ingests.

Date & Time: 2026-09-21 14:07:10
Location: [Insert Location]
Customer: Lance
## Overview
This consultation summary covers a discussion between Lance and Maddie Savoy of Kip and King Marketing regarding social media content creation services for car dealerships. Lance is seeking high-quality, cinematic video and photography rather than "goofy" viral-style content. Topics included content types, pricing, and Lance’s need for content creation only—no social media management—since he already uses a syndicated posting system. The core challenge is aligning the agency’s standard package pricing with a content-only request.
## Background
Lance, who manages or consults for car dealerships, is evaluating Kip and King Marketing’s services. He uses an automated system that posts to social channels via Google Drive, so he does not want full social media management. He strongly prefers cinematic-style video (e.g., Ferrari dealership examples) over trendy or “dumb” viral content. He aims to understand the value and pricing for content creation he can feed into his existing system.
## Pain Points
The primary issue is the misalignment between the agency’s bundled service and Lance’s content-only needs. His syndicated posting system makes management/posting redundant. He stated, “I don’t need it posted or managed... that really is just literal content creation.” Paying $1,750 per month for unused services creates a value concern. The agency’s initial stance that pricing would remain unchanged does not address his need, pushing him toward an ill-suited package.
## Expectations
Lance wants a customized, content-only pricing model. He expects a set number of high-quality photos and video reels per month delivered via Google Drive for his system to handle. He is interested in roughly 20 assets monthly, including one video reel per week (four per month), and seeks a fair price solely for asset creation—excluding management, scheduling, and posting. Success is a quote reflecting this reduced scope.
## Other Information Summary
- Kip and King Marketing has an in-house photographer and videographer who travel for shoots.
- The standard package is $1,750 per month per dealership.
- It includes one site visit per month and delivers about five posts per week, including photography, graphics, and one video reel weekly.
- Maddie Savoy is local to Lance’s area.
- Lance prefers high-quality, cinematic content over “goofy” or “dumb” viral videos, while acknowledging that style works for some dealerships (e.g., one in Texas).
## To-Do List
- [ ] Follow up with Maddie Savoy at Kip and King Marketing to negotiate a content-only price.
- [ ] Define exact deliverables (photo count vs. video count) for a custom package.
- [ ] Request cinematic video samples to confirm brand alignment.
> **AI Suggestions**
> The AI has identified the client’s main pain point as the mismatch between the bundled package and the content-only need. Potential solutions:
> 1. Propose an “Asset-Only” package. Itemize costs for content creation (pre-production, shooting, editing) versus management (scheduling, posting, reporting) and remove management fees to reduce price.
> 2. Offer a tiered content menu. Options like “10 photos + 2 reels for $X” or “15 photos + 4 reels for $Y” provide flexibility without paying for unwanted services.
> 3. Suggest a pilot or per-visit model. Offer a one-time content shoot at a fixed price so Lance can assess quality and workflow with his system before committing to a retainer.

recordings.summary_md:
## 1. Weekly Lead and Service Appointment Reporting Workflow
The team aims to streamline how salespeople receive and work lead and service appointment lists. Current pain points include fragmented sources across “so many different platforms,” duplicated or mis-categorized sold records (e.g., “Amy Lambert” vs. “Andy/Amy Lambert”), and manual printing/updating that frustrates the team. Centralizing into one customizable list mitigates inefficiency, ensures coverage of “service appointments into the future” and “old leads,” and supports targeted follow-up. Proposed solutions include a weekly Monday print and/or automated email with PDFs, configurable filters (remove solds, 90 or 180 days, “today plus future,” “all loaded days”), and tailoring to profitable trades and sweet spots (e.g., 22–24 BMWs, model search like “230/240/250”). Automation leverages existing system data and CSV report emailing via Event Solutions to agents, reducing manual overhead and increasing engagement.
### Action Items
- [ ] Set a weekly cadence to generate and distribute a consolidated list every Monday, covering service appointments for the week and active leads, with “today plus future” and “all loaded days” toggle options -- *Lance* 2026-09-21
- [ ] Implement a “Remove Solds” filter with configurable sold-removal windows (90 or 180 days), while allowing teams to keep certain solds when appropriate -- *Lance* 2026-09-23
- [ ] Configure an automated Monday morning email per salesperson with a PDF of their weekly service appointments -- *Lance* 2026-09-23
